title: CPT Purpose and Structure

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the purpose of CPT as the standardized code set for reporting medical, surgical, and diagnostic procedures and services.
- Describe the structure of CPT, including Category I, Category II, and Category III codes and the six Category I sections.
- Recognize that the AMA owns and licenses CPT and apply the limits on reproducing proprietary code content in educational and workplace use.
- Distinguish procedure coding (CPT) from diagnosis coding and explain how modifiers, add-on codes, and HCPCS levels support accurate claims.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

CPT is like a special dictionary of numbers that doctors and offices use to name exactly what service they gave a patient, and the letters stand for Current Procedural Terminology.

### Question 2

CPT is like a menu with a number for every kind of service a doctor can do, so everyone reads the same number and knows exactly what happened.

### Question 3

The American Medical Association is like the publisher of the procedure-code dictionary; they write and update the number list every year.

### Question 4

Think of it like a receipt: CPT is the item the store sold (the service), and the diagnosis code is the reason the customer needed it (the illness).

### Question 5

Category I codes are like the main phone numbers in the book: five digits long, plain numbers, used for the everyday services.

### Question 6

HCPCS is a big filing cabinet with two drawers; the top drawer (Level I) holds CPT procedure codes, and the second drawer holds supply codes.

### Question 7

The CPT book is split into six chapters, one for each big group of services, like a library has separate shelves for different subjects.

### Question 8

Category II codes are like checkmarks on a quality checklist; they help a clinic show it is doing good work, but they are not how the clinic gets paid.

### Question 9

Category II codes wear the letter F like a name tag that says 'this one is for tracking quality.'

### Question 10

Category III codes are like a 'test run' label for brand-new medical services, so everyone can gather information about them before they become regular codes.

### Question 11

Category III codes wear the letter T like a name tag that says 'temporary' or 'new and being tested.'

### Question 12

Medicare, like a store's checkout system, needs the standard CPT number for each service so it knows what to pay for.

### Question 13

Every January, the procedure-code dictionary gets a new edition with some new numbers and some old numbers retired, like an updated edition of a phone book.

### Question 14

The AMA is like the author of the code book; it owns the words and numbers, and other people need permission to use them.

### Question 15

The 'Evaluation and Management' chapter is like the front desk of the code book, covering everyday check-ups and office visits.

### Question 16

A modifier is like a sticky note attached to a code that adds a detail, such as 'this was on the left side' or 'this was a separate service.'

### Question 17

An add-on code is like a side dish on a menu: you can only order it along with a main dish, never by itself.

### Question 18

Category II codes are like a report card the office fills out voluntarily to show quality, not a way to charge for a service.

### Question 19

Standardized codes are like everyone speaking the same language, so a code means the same thing to every doctor, office, and insurance company.

### Question 20

The CPT Editorial Panel is like the editors of the code book, deciding which new numbers to add and which old ones to retire.

### Question 21

Each five-digit CPT number is like a bar code that names one particular service a provider performs.

### Question 22

The six sections of the CPT book are like six labeled shelves, and 'Radiology' is one of those shelf names.

### Question 23

The code is the noun that names the service, and the modifier is an adjective tacked on to describe a special circumstance.

### Question 24

If a code has a letter in it, it is one of the special helper codes (Category II or III), not a regular five-number Category I code.

### Question 25

E/M codes are the codes for the doctor's visit itself: talking with, examining, and planning care for a patient.

### Question 26

A well-known, everyday service gets a regular five-digit Category I number, the 'standard' code.

### Question 27

For a brand-new service that is still being tested, CPT uses a temporary Category III 'learner' code so everyone can gather information about it.

### Question 28

Category II codes are the 'quality checklist' codes a clinic uses to show it is meeting care goals.

### Question 29

The procedure code is the 'what we did' number, and that is a CPT Category I code.

### Question 30

If you cannot find the right number, ask the coding expert instead of making one up; guessing can cause big problems later.

### Question 31

The encounter form has two labeled columns: one for 'what we did' (CPT) and one for 'why' (the diagnosis code).

### Question 32

A new, experimental service is like a brand-new product a store might not accept a coupon for yet; the office has to check whether the plan covers it.

### Question 33

Using the code book is like using a copyrighted song in a video; the office or software company needs permission (a license) from the owner.

### Question 34

Learning about how the code system works is like learning about a book; but you still cannot photocopy the whole book without the author's permission.

### Question 35

Using a number from an old edition of the code book is like sending a letter with a retired zip code; it may come back undelivered.

### Question 36

Level II codes are the 'extra items' codes for things like medical supplies and equipment that do not have a CPT number.

### Question 37

Reading and explaining an X-ray or scan is the 'Radiology' chapter of the code book.

### Question 38

The 'Surgery' chapter is where operations and surgical procedures get their codes.

### Question 39

The 'Pathology and Laboratory' chapter is the place for tests done on samples, like blood draws and lab panels.

### Question 40

The 'Anesthesiology' chapter is for the medicine that keeps a patient asleep and pain-free during surgery.

### Question 41

The 'Medicine' chapter is like the catch-all shelf for many non-surgical treatments, including shots like vaccines.

### Question 42

When every office uses the same numbers, researchers can add up the numbers from many places to spot patterns in health care.

### Question 43

A modifier is like flagging two separate items on a receipt so the cashier knows to ring them up as two purchases, not one.

### Question 44

A modifier is a short two-character tag that gets attached to the end of a five-digit code.

### Question 45

An add-on code is the side dish that must be ordered with the main dish; it cannot be served by itself.

### Question 46

Choosing the right code is a job for the trained coding expert or the clinician, with the assistant helping gather information along the way.

### Question 47

The Editorial Panel is the group of experts who decide what new numbers go into the code book each year.

### Question 48

Everyone using the same code numbers is like every store scanning the same barcodes, so checkout works everywhere.

### Question 49

The assistant can explain that the doctor writes down what happened and then the coding team picks the matching number, like a chef writes the recipe before the price tag is made.

### Question 50

The code comes from what the doctor actually wrote down and did, like a receipt being made from what was really purchased.

### Question 51

The assistant is like a helpful assistant in the coding kitchen, gathering and checking ingredients while the trained chef decides the final recipe.

### Question 52

Category III codes are on probation; after a while, the editors decide whether the service has proven itself and earns a permanent number, or gets dropped.

### Question 53

A letter inside the code is a clue that it is a special helper code, not one of the regular five-number procedure codes.

### Question 54

A proprietary code set is like a copyrighted book; the author owns it, and others need permission before copying it.

### Question 55

The superbill has two columns: one with 'what was done' numbers and one with 'why' numbers.

### Question 56

CPT is 'what,' the diagnosis is 'why,' and the modifier is the extra detail like 'left side' or 'separate visit.'

### Question 57

Before submitting, the office checks whether the insurance plan will pay for the new service, like checking a store's return policy before buying.

### Question 58

Insurance companies need the standard code, like a barcode at a store, so their computers know exactly what service to pay for.

### Question 59

The diagnosis is the 'why' that makes the 'what' (the procedure) make sense, like a doctor's note explaining why a test was needed.

### Question 60

The diagnosis is the reason on the form that explains why the procedure was needed.

### Question 61

The assistant checks the newest edition of the code book, like checking today's schedule instead of last year's.

### Question 62

Category II codes are the 'report card' codes that are not used to get paid, unlike the regular and new-service codes.

### Question 63

When a supply does not have a regular CPT number, the office uses the 'Level II' supply codes instead.

### Question 64

A modifier is like adding a note to a receipt; the note adds detail but does not change what was actually bought.

### Question 65

To check a number, use the newest code book, just as you would check the newest map for current roads.

### Question 66

A superbill is like the receipt that lists what services happened, so the billing team can turn it into a claim.

### Question 67

Repairing a cut is a surgical service, so its code lives in the 'Surgery' chapter.

### Question 68

When a claim comes back rejected, the assistant flags it for the billing experts instead of guessing, so the office handles it the right way.

### Question 69

Each separate service gets its own line on the receipt, with a note (modifier) showing they are not the same thing.

### Question 70

Putting the code book inside an app is like putting a copyrighted song in a game; the maker needs a license from the owner first.

### Question 71

You can teach people the idea in your own words, but you should not photocopy the whole copyrighted book and hand it out.

### Question 72

Saying a service was bigger than it really was, just to get more money, is like overcharging a customer on purpose; it is not allowed.

### Question 73

When the number is missing, the assistant hands it to the coding expert, who reads what the doctor wrote and picks the right number.

### Question 74

You use the number that was valid on the day the service happened, like using last year's calendar for a date in December.

### Question 75

Category II is the 'report card' code (no payment), and Category III is the 'new service' code that might be billed if the plan covers it.

### Question 76

When all offices use the same numbers, researchers can add them up across the country to spot health trends, like counting the same kind of coin in many piggy banks.

### Question 77

The AMA writes the code book, and CMS (which runs Medicare) says 'we will use that book for our programs.'

### Question 78

A service that proves itself over time can earn a permanent number, like an intern being promoted to a permanent job.

### Question 79

When there is no exact number for a service, the office uses the 'unlisted' code, like a 'miscellaneous' line on a form.

### Question 80

For a 'miscellaneous' code, the office must attach a written explanation of what was done, like attaching a note to a mystery item in a box.

### Question 81

Using the wrong number on purpose is like putting the wrong price tag on an item; it may cause trouble and does not describe what really happened.

### Question 82

If an assistant sees something that could be wrong, the right move is to tell the boss, like telling a teacher when something is not right.

### Question 83

Level II codes are for the 'extra stuff' like equipment and some services, while CPT handles the doctor's procedures.

### Question 84

The 'why' (diagnosis) has to match the 'what' (procedure), like a receipt where the reason for the purchase explains the purchase itself.

### Question 85

The code book gets updated every year because medicine keeps inventing new tests and treatments, so the numbers need to keep up.
